screens.title: What is Network Automation?
screens.narratorSegment: Network automation is the practice of using software to perform configuration, deployment, testing, and operational tasks across network devices. Put simply, automation replaces repetitive manual CLI work with scripts and programs that can run reliably at scale. A concrete example is configuring an NTP server and a login banner on 15 devices; where manual CLI requires logging into each device and typing commands, an automated approach describes the desired state once and applies it to all devices uniformly. Automation's primary benefits include speed—changes that once took hours can often be completed in minutes—consistency—scripts enforce identical configurations across devices—and reduced human error, which translates to improved network reliability. One common misconception is that automation removes the need to understand the network; in reality, automation requires stronger design thinking because errors scale faster. Always test automation in a lab and use small, incremental rollouts. Takeaway: automation multiplies your effectiveness but also demands disciplined testing and secure practices. screens.title: Manual CLI vs Automated Programmatic Approaches
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between manual CLI work and automated programmatic approaches is central to making good design choices. Manual CLI is imperative: you log into a device and issue step-by-step commands that tell the device exactly how to change its state. For example, to set an IP address you type a sequence of commands for each interface. This approach is immediate and familiar, but it is slow and prone to inconsistent typing or omissions across many devices. Programmatic approaches use APIs and structured models to interact with devices. An A P I call or a playbook describes operations in a consistent format; a declarative model describes the desired end state and lets the automation system figure out the steps. One common misconception is that declarative approaches hide details; they do abstract the steps, but you still need to understand networking to design correct desired states. A practical rule: use imperative methods for one-off troubleshooting, and prefer declarative automation for repeated, large-scale configuration to ensure consistency. What's one change you currently make repeatedly that could benefit from a declarative definition? Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Manual CLI vs Automated
Manual, Imperative
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
no shutdown
exit
This sequence is explicit and device-specific. It works well for single fixes but becomes repetitive and error-prone across many devices.
Misconception
Imperative commands are always safer. They are immediate but risk inconsistent results when repeated manually.
Declarative / Programmatic
{
  "interface": "GigabitEthernet0/1",
  "ip": "192.168.1.1/24",
  "admin": "up"
}
A declarative description states desired state; the automation engine determines steps to apply it. This is repeatable and easier to validate across many devices.
Key Takeaway

Use imperative for ad-hoc fixes; prefer declarative for consistent, large-scale configuration management.

screens.title: What is an API in Networking?
screens.narratorSegment: An A P I is a defined interface that lets software request information or actions from another system in a predictable, structured way. In networking, APIs expose device capabilities—querying status, retrieving counters, or applying configurations—using structured data such as JSON or XML. This contrasts with human-readable CLI output, which is designed for people and can be brittle to parse automatically. A concrete example: instead of parsing free-form 'show' output to find an interface status, an A P I returns a structured field you can read programmatically. APIs reduce errors because they enforce types and structure; when you request a specific configuration change, the A P I responds with clear success or failure messages. A common misconception is that APIs are always available on every device. In practice, older devices may lack modern APIs or may support specific protocols like NETCONF or RESTCONF instead. The practical takeaway is to inventory device A P I capabilities and prefer APIs where available to make automation robust and maintainable. In practical terms, apis as structured interfaces replacing fragile cli scraping. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

APIs return structured data
{
  "interfaces": [
    {"name": "GigabitEthernet0/1", "admin": "up", "ip": "192.168.1.1"}

screens.title: NETCONF and YANG
screens.narratorSegment: NETCONF and YANG are closely related technologies that provide structured configuration and state management for network devices. NETCONF is a protocol designed to install, manipulate, and delete configuration; it uses XML encoding and relies on structured data models to represent settings. YANG is the data modeling language that defines the shape and constraints of configuration and operational data—think of YANG as the schema and NETCONF as the mechanism to read or write data that matches that schema. A concrete example is a YANG model defining an interface object with fields for name, IP, and admin state; NETCONF operates against that model to apply or retrieve those values. A common misconception is that NETCONF alone enforces correctness; in truth, you still need correct YANG models and validation in your automation pipeline. NETCONF and YANG together make configuration less fragile and easier to validate programmatically, which is why they are foundational for robust network programmability. Key practice: inspect available YANG models on devices and test NETCONF operations in a lab before production. NETCONF and YANG means yang defines structured models; netconf uses these models to reliably change and retrieve device configuration using xml-encoded exchanges.. In practical terms, how netconf and yang work together to model and change device state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › NETCONF & YANG
YANG example (conceptual)
module example-interface {
  container interfaces {
    list interface {
      leaf name { type string; }
      leaf ip { type string; }
      leaf admin { type enumeration { enum up; enum down; }}
    }
  }
}
YANG defines the structure and allowed values for configuration data so automation can validate input before applying it.
NETCONF role
NETCONF uses XML-encoded RPC calls against YANG-modeled data to get or set configuration. Together they remove ambiguity and support validation.
Why it matters
Structured models and protocol-level operations make programmatic changes predictable and testable.

screens.title: RESTCONF
screens.narratorSegment: RESTCONF is an HTTP-based protocol that exposes device configuration and operational data using RESTful principles and often the same YANG models used with NETCONF. It provides a web-friendly interface to read and write structured data, typically using JSON or XML payloads. For example, a RESTCONF GET request returns interface data in JSON matching the YANG model, which a script can parse directly. RESTCONF is a useful alternative where an HTTP-based toolchain or web integrations are preferable. A common misconception is that RESTCONF always returns JSON; while JSON is common, some implementations may use XML depending on the YANG model and device support. In practice, RESTCONF simplifies integration with web frameworks and monitoring platforms because it uses familiar HTTP verbs and status codes. When choosing between NETCONF and RESTCONF, consider your existing tooling and the device support—both rely on YANG models for structured, reliable interaction. RESTCONF means restconf is an http-based interface to yang-modeled device data, making device interactions accessible via restful calls and json/xml payloads.. In practical terms, http-based access to yang-modeled data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

RESTCONF request example (conceptual)
GET /restconf/data/interfaces/interface=GigabitEthernet0/1
Accept: application/yang-data+json

Response 200 OK
{
  "interface": { "name": "GigabitEthernet0/1", "admin": "up" }

RESTCONF uses HTTP verbs and can return JSON that directly maps to YANG models, simplifying parsing in scripts.

screens.title: Python and Ansible in Network Automation
screens.narratorSegment: Python and Ansible are two common pillars in network automation. Python is a general-purpose scripting language used to interact with APIs, process structured outputs, and build automation tools. Ansible is an agentless automation engine that uses YAML playbooks to express desired changes and can call APIs or use SSH to configure devices. A concrete illustration: you might write a Python script that calls a RESTCONF endpoint to check interface status and then generate a report. Alternatively, an Ansible playbook can declare a set of configuration tasks—like ensuring NTP is set—and run them across many devices in a single command. A common misconception is that Ansible is only for servers; it is widely used for network devices because it is agentless and supports network modules. When using Python, prefer libraries and patterns that handle retries and errors; when using Ansible, structure playbooks and inventory to keep secrets safe. Both tools can coexist: use Python for custom data processing and Ansible for repeatable configuration runs. Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Python & Ansible
Python: conceptual snippet
import requests
url = 'https://device/restconf/data/interfaces'
resp = requests.get(url, auth=('user','pass'), verify=False)
if resp.status_code == 200:
  data = resp.json()
  # process interface data
This shows a simple REST call pattern: request, check status, parse JSON, and act on structured data.
Ansible: conceptual playbook
- name: Configure NTP on switches
  hosts: switches
  gather_facts: no
  tasks:
    - name: Ensure NTP server is set
      ios_config:
        lines: - ntp server 192.168.10.10

screens.title: Imperative vs Declarative Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: The distinction between imperative and declarative configuration is important when designing automation. Imperative approaches tell the system exactly how to change state step by step. This is useful for troubleshooting or very specific device commands you want to control tightly. A concrete example is manually entering interface commands when debugging connectivity. Declarative approaches, by contrast, describe the desired end state—such as 'VLAN 100 named DATA exists'—and the automation engine figures out the necessary steps. Declarative is powerful for consistent, repeatable tasks across many devices, reducing human variation. A common misconception is that declarative systems remove the need to understand the resulting commands; they do not. Engineers must still reason about dependencies, order of operations, and potential conflicts. Practical guidance: use imperative commands during targeted fixes and use declarative definitions for provisioning and ongoing state management. screens.title: Safe Adoption: Start Small, Test, Secure
screens.narratorSegment: Adopting automation safely is a process: start small, test thoroughly, secure credentials, and roll out progressively. Begin by selecting low-risk, repetitive tasks—examples include NTP server configuration, banner messages, or standard SNMP settings—so you can prove value without exposing critical infrastructure to risk. Next, build a test environment or use a staging subset of devices. Validate your scripts or playbooks, and include automated tests that verify the desired state after changes. Secure credential handling is essential: do not store plaintext credentials in scripts. Use a vault or credential manager and role-based access to the automation system. When moving to production, deploy changes gradually and monitor closely for unexpected effects. One common mistake is trying to automate every task at once; that creates complexity and hides problems. The practical takeaway is incremental progress: each small, validated automation builds trust and frees engineering time for higher-value work. screens.title: Monitoring, Validation and Rollback Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Verification and the ability to roll back are essential parts of safe automation. After applying a configuration, always run automated validation to confirm the device state matches the desired state; for example, check that NTP peers are reachable and that the banner text is present. Use simple programmatic checks that return success or failure so your automation can stop or alert if something is wrong. Monitoring telemetry and logs helps detect unintended effects; automated monitoring can surface anomalies faster than manual checks. For rollback, keep versioned backups of device configuration and design playbooks or scripts to revert changes if validation fails. A common error is assuming a change succeeded because the automation reported completion; instead, rely on post-change validations that query device state via APIs or verified CLI checks. The practical workflow is: dry-run, apply, validate, monitor, and be prepared to rollback using an audited configuration snapshot. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this chapter you will learn why networks are moving from manual command-line work toward automation and programmability, and how that change affects daily operations. We begin by defining network automation as the use of software to configure, test, deploy, and operate physical and virtual network devices. You will hear concrete reasons for adopting automation: faster changes across many devices, consistent and repeatable configurations, fewer human mistakes, and better operational efficiency. I will also introduce the main enabling pieces: APIs that expose device functions, protocols and data models such as NETCONF, RESTCONF, and YANG, and widely used tools like Python and Ansible. You'll see a simple analogy: think of an A P I as a restaurant menu that lets you order a dish instead of walking into the kitchen and cooking it yourself. Finally, we'll preview the practical activity where you plan a small automation to push an NTP server and a banner to many devices. As you progress, ask yourself: which repetitive task on your network could you automate first?

In this first set of objectives we focus on the foundational knowledge you need to reason about automation. First, you will explain the fundamental concepts and benefits of network automation: why automation speeds work, reduces errors, and improves reliability. For example, deploying a consistent NTP configuration to many switches takes minutes with automation instead of hours. Second, you will differentiate traditional network management from modern automated approaches. That means understanding the difference between logging into devices and issuing step-by-step CLI commands versus using programmatic APIs and intent-driven descriptions. Third, you will identify key components and protocols that enable programmability, such as NETCONF, RESTCONF, and YANG, and you will be able to say when a structured data model helps avoid fragile screen-scraping of CLI output. Fourth, you will recognize core tools commonly used, like Python for scripting and Ansible for agentless playbooks, and why each tool is useful. Each objective relates to practical decision-making: which tasks to automate, which protocols to learn, and which tools to pilot first.

In this second set of objectives we move from knowledge into practical judgment and safe practices. First, you will understand the distinction between imperative and declarative approaches so you can choose the right method for a task; for example, step-by-step CLI changes are imperative, while describing a VLAN state for an automation system is declarative. Second, you will learn to identify automation opportunities and plan an approach — the hands-on activity guides you through choosing NTP and banner changes to automate across multiple devices. Third, you will recognize common adoption challenges such as learning curve, security of credentials, and inadequate testing, and you will be able to explain mitigation steps like credential vaults and progressive rollout. Fourth, you will be able to outline a basic, safe automation workflow: test in lab, validate in staging, apply to production carefully, and monitor the results. These skills help you not only write scripts but also integrate automation into real operational processes.

Network automation is the practice of using software to perform configuration, deployment, testing, and operational tasks across network devices. Put simply, automation replaces repetitive manual CLI work with scripts and programs that can run reliably at scale. A concrete example is configuring an NTP server and a login banner on 15 devices; where manual CLI requires logging into each device and typing commands, an automated approach describes the desired state once and applies it to all devices uniformly. Automation's primary benefits include speed—changes that once took hours can often be completed in minutes—consistency—scripts enforce identical configurations across devices—and reduced human error, which translates to improved network reliability. One common misconception is that automation removes the need to understand the network; in reality, automation requires stronger design thinking because errors scale faster. Always test automation in a lab and use small, incremental rollouts. Takeaway: automation multiplies your effectiveness but also demands disciplined testing and secure practices. Which routine task in your network would you automate first? What is Network Automation? means automation uses software to perform and repeat network tasks reliably, improving speed, consistency, and reliability.. In practical terms, definition, scope, and immediate benefits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the difference between manual CLI work and automated programmatic approaches is central to making good design choices. Manual CLI is imperative: you log into a device and issue step-by-step commands that tell the device exactly how to change its state. For example, to set an IP address you type a sequence of commands for each interface. This approach is immediate and familiar, but it is slow and prone to inconsistent typing or omissions across many devices. Programmatic approaches use APIs and structured models to interact with devices. An A P I call or a playbook describes operations in a consistent format; a declarative model describes the desired end state and lets the automation system figure out the steps. One common misconception is that declarative approaches hide details; they do abstract the steps, but you still need to understand networking to design correct desired states. A practical rule: use imperative methods for one-off troubleshooting, and prefer declarative automation for repeated, large-scale configuration to ensure consistency. What's one change you currently make repeatedly that could benefit from a declarative definition? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An A P I is a defined interface that lets software request information or actions from another system in a predictable, structured way. In networking, APIs expose device capabilities—querying status, retrieving counters, or applying configurations—using structured data such as JSON or XML. This contrasts with human-readable CLI output, which is designed for people and can be brittle to parse automatically. A concrete example: instead of parsing free-form 'show' output to find an interface status, an A P I returns a structured field you can read programmatically. APIs reduce errors because they enforce types and structure; when you request a specific configuration change, the A P I responds with clear success or failure messages. A common misconception is that APIs are always available on every device. In practice, older devices may lack modern APIs or may support specific protocols like NETCONF or RESTCONF instead. The practical takeaway is to inventory device A P I capabilities and prefer APIs where available to make automation robust and maintainable. What is an API in Networking? means apis provide structured, machine-friendly access to device functions, enabling reliable automation without brittle text parsing.. In practical terms, apis as structured interfaces replacing fragile cli scraping. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

NETCONF and YANG are closely related technologies that provide structured configuration and state management for network devices. NETCONF is a protocol designed to install, manipulate, and delete configuration; it uses XML encoding and relies on structured data models to represent settings. YANG is the data modeling language that defines the shape and constraints of configuration and operational data—think of YANG as the schema and NETCONF as the mechanism to read or write data that matches that schema. A concrete example is a YANG model defining an interface object with fields for name, IP, and admin state; NETCONF operates against that model to apply or retrieve those values. A common misconception is that NETCONF alone enforces correctness; in truth, you still need correct YANG models and validation in your automation pipeline. NETCONF and YANG together make configuration less fragile and easier to validate programmatically, which is why they are foundational for robust network programmability. Key practice: inspect available YANG models on devices and test NETCONF operations in a lab before production. NETCONF and YANG means yang defines structured models; netconf uses these models to reliably change and retrieve device configuration using xml-encoded exchanges.. In practical terms, how netconf and yang work together to model and change device state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

RESTCONF is an HTTP-based protocol that exposes device configuration and operational data using RESTful principles and often the same YANG models used with NETCONF. It provides a web-friendly interface to read and write structured data, typically using JSON or XML payloads. For example, a RESTCONF GET request returns interface data in JSON matching the YANG model, which a script can parse directly. RESTCONF is a useful alternative where an HTTP-based toolchain or web integrations are preferable. A common misconception is that RESTCONF always returns JSON; while JSON is common, some implementations may use XML depending on the YANG model and device support. In practice, RESTCONF simplifies integration with web frameworks and monitoring platforms because it uses familiar HTTP verbs and status codes. When choosing between NETCONF and RESTCONF, consider your existing tooling and the device support—both rely on YANG models for structured, reliable interaction. Python and Ansible are two common pillars in network automation. Python is a general-purpose scripting language used to interact with APIs, process structured outputs, and build automation tools. Ansible is an agentless automation engine that uses YAML playbooks to express desired changes and can call APIs or use SSH to configure devices. A concrete illustration: you might write a Python script that calls a RESTCONF endpoint to check interface status and then generate a report. Declarative approaches, by contrast, describe the desired end state—such as 'VLAN 100 named DATA exists'—and the automation engine figures out the necessary steps. Declarative is powerful for consistent, repeatable tasks across many devices, reducing human variation. Practical guidance: use imperative commands during targeted fixes and use declarative definitions for provisioning and ongoing state management. Adopting automation safely is a process: start small, test thoroughly, secure credentials, and roll out progressively. Verification and the ability to roll back are essential parts of safe automation. After applying a configuration, always run automated validation to confirm the device state matches the desired state; for example, check that NTP peers are reachable and that the banner text is present. Use simple programmatic checks that return success or failure so your automation can stop or alert if something is wrong. Monitoring telemetry and logs helps detect unintended effects; automated monitoring can surface anomalies faster than manual checks. For rollback, keep versioned backups of device configuration and design playbooks or scripts to revert changes if validation fails. A common error is assuming a change succeeded because the automation reported completion; instead, rely on post-change validations that query device state via APIs or verified CLI checks. The practical workflow is: dry-run, apply, validate, monitor, and be prepared to rollback using an audited configuration snapshot. Let's review three core concepts that anchor this chapter. First, network automation is the practice of using software to automate configuration, testing, deployment, and operations to achieve speed, consistency, and reduced human error. Second, network programmability is the ability to manage devices and services programmatically through structured interfaces like APIs, which replace fragile parsing of CLI outputs with predictable data. Third, an A P I is a defined interface that allows different software to communicate; in networking it exposes device functions and state as structured data, enabling reliable automation. Keep these ideas in mind: automation is not magic—it is an engineering discipline that requires testing and security. To close, remember three supporting technical concepts that enable modern network programmability. NETCONF is a protocol that performs configuration operations using XML and YANG models. RESTCONF provides an HTTP-based, RESTful interface to YANG-modeled data, often returning JSON that is simple to integrate with web tools. YANG itself is the data modeling language that defines the structure, types, and constraints for device configuration and state information. Together these technologies make device data predictable and automatable. A common pitfall is assuming all devices support the same models; before automating, inventory device capabilities and test model availability.
